attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

"""exp-008 v3: Binary Probe GRPO -- ablation cascade member.

Ablation cascade:
  exp-003: R3-only (no R1)
  exp-008 v3: Binary Probe R1 (this script)
  exp-014: Continuous Probe R1
  exp-002: Directional Projection R1 (full DC-GRPO)

Replaces R1 (direction projection) with a binary logistic regression probe.
R1 = 1.0 if P(sycophantic) <= 0.5, else 0.0. The probe is retrained every
500 steps on the current model's activations to track representation drift.
"""

import json

def edit_paper_section(
    project: str,
    section: str,
    old_text: str,
    new_text: str,
    claims: list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None,
    table_cells: list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None,
    figures: list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None,
) -> ToolResult:
    """Edit a paper section with whitespace-normalized matching.

    Args:
        project: Project name.
        section: Section name.
        old_text: Text to find (whitespace-normalized matching).
        new_text: Replacement text.
        claims: Claim updates (match by text → replace evidence; new → add).
        table_cells: Table cell updates (by table_id + row + col).
        figures: Figure updates (by figure_id).

    Returns:
        ToolResult with updated section info.
    """
    if not project:
        return ToolResult(success=False, error="project is required")

    lock_path = _get_lock_path(project)
    lock_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    lock_fd = open(lock_path, "a+")
    try:
        fcntl.flock(lock_fd, fcntl.LOCK_EX)
        return _edit_paper_section_locked(project, section, old_text, new_text, claims, table_cells, figures)
    finally:
        fcntl.flock(lock_fd, fcntl.LOCK_UN)
        lock_fd.close()

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation extends beyond Qwen3-8B: Llama-3-8B independently achieves AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$ on the same contrastive pairs with the same monotonic evidence gradient, so discriminability generalizes across architectures while the semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions applied via advantage modification in GRPO achieve 100\% validation accuracy for reward hacking detection, where shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
A quantitative comparison of geometric separability between $\dsyc$ and their reward-hacking directions remains an important open question.
Independently, \citet{kelkar2026persona} find that persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ in activation space, further suggesting that $\dsyc$ does not encode the full semantic structure of sycophancy.
The multi-dimensional decomposition of sycophancy into independently steerable sub-behaviors~\citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} compounds this limitation: $\dsyc$ projects distinct sub-phenomena onto a single axis, amplifying the warranted-vs-unwarranted ambiguity.
For sycophancy, the target and its complement occupy the same activation region; they differ only in whether external evidence warrants the belief change.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy using a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) via Best-of-N reranking without producing gradients.
